prompt: In the teleport demo, where did the note written inside `<Teleport to="body">` end up?
hint: Look at the last line of the printed body.

choices.text: As the last element of `<body>`, outside `#app` altogether
choices.why: Right. It comes after the `<script>` tag, beyond the end of `#app`.

choices.text: Inside the card's `<div>`, after the first note
choices.why: That is where the other note stayed, the one written outside the Teleport.

choices.text: Inside `#app`, as the next sibling of the card's `<div>`
choices.why: The transcript closes `#app` first; the note is after the `<script>` tag.

choices.text: Between the two comments, `teleport start` and `teleport end`
choices.why: The comments are empty: they only mark where the Teleport was written.

prompt: The teleported note still carries `data-v-9092e573`. Why?

choices.text: Vue copies the attributes of `<Teleport>` onto its contents
choices.why: The Teleport here has only `to`; the attribute is the card's scoped-style mark.

choices.text: The body takes the scoped id of the last component that teleported into it
choices.why: The `<body>` itself carries no such attribute in the transcript; only the card's elements do.

choices.text: It is still the card's markup, so the card's scoped styles reach it
choices.why: Right. Only the elements moved; the component that wrote them did not change.

choices.text: It is a leftover Vue forgets to remove when an element moves
choices.why: Nothing was forgotten: the attribute is there on purpose, because the note is still the card's.

prompt: A menu is written inside a card and must sit on top of the whole page. Which rules on the card are reasons, by the lesson, to teleport it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which of these clip, and which create a layer?

choices.text: `overflow: hidden` with a fixed height
choices.why: Right. That is the demo's card, and the note inside it was cut off at its edge.

choices.text: `color: #1d2b24`
choices.why: A colour is inherited by the text and neither clips nor makes a layer.

choices.text: `transform: scale(1.02)`
choices.why: Right. A `transform` on any ancestor creates a layer the menu is trapped in.

choices.text: `font-family: system-ui`
choices.why: The menu inherits the face, and nothing about its position changes.

choices.text: `filter: blur(1px)`
choices.why: Right. The lesson names `filter` beside `transform`: each one makes a new layer.

prompt: In the dialog demo, which line of the component moves the focus to `#minutes` when the dialog opens?

choices.text: `aria-labelledby="dialog-title"`
choices.why: That gives the dialog a name for a screen reader; it moves nothing.

choices.text: The `@close` listener, which also runs on every open
choices.why: `close` fires when the dialog closes, and it only logged where the focus had gone back to.

choices.text: The `value="30"` on the field, which marks it as the first
choices.why: A value fills the field; it says nothing about the focus.

choices.text: None; `showModal()` does it
choices.why: Right. The browser moved the focus inside, and back out on closing, with no line of the demo asking.

prompt: The dialog was closed once with Escape and once with *Add*. What did `returnValue` hold each time?

choices.text: `"cancel"`, then `"add"`
choices.why: Escape pressed no button, so the Cancel button's value was never given.

choices.text: `""`, then `"add"`
choices.why: Right. Escape leaves it empty; a button in a `<form method="dialog">` closes it with its own `value`.

choices.text: `"Escape"`, then `"Add"`
choices.why: `returnValue` is a button's `value`, not the name of a key or the text on a button.

choices.text: `null` the first time, because a key is not a form, then `"add"`
choices.why: It is a string, and the transcript printed an empty one: `closed with ""`.

prompt: Somebody opens the planner's dialog with `dialog.show()` instead of `showModal()`. What do they lose?
hint: Read the last paragraph of the section.

choices.text: Nothing, because both put the dialog on the top layer and differ only in the backdrop
choices.why: Only `showModal()` uses the top layer; `show()` draws an ordinary box in the page.

choices.text: Only the template ref, which `show()` cannot use
choices.why: Both are methods of the same element, called through the same ref.

choices.text: The top layer, and with it the inert page behind: it becomes an ordinary box
choices.why: Right. Opened with `show()` it is a box in the page, and the rest of the page stays live.

choices.text: The `<form method="dialog">`, which then submits to the server
choices.why: The form's method belongs to the form; it closes the dialog whichever way it was opened.

prompt: What makes `SlowCourse` an async component?

choices.text: Being written inside a `<Suspense>`
choices.why: Suspense waits for async components; it does not make one. Without the `await`, it would have nothing to wait for.

choices.text: Its `onMounted`, which logs after the data has arrived
choices.why: The hook runs after mounting, which is too late to hold the drawing back.

choices.text: The `await` at the top level of `<script setup>`
choices.why: Right. A setup that awaits cannot be drawn until it has finished.

choices.text: The `id` prop, which is a string read from the parent
choices.why: A prop is synchronous; `SuspenseDemo` passes it as plain text.

prompt: The dev server showed what the compiler made of `SlowCourse`. How many calls to `_withAsyncContext` did `grep` find in its body, not counting the import?
`SlowCourse` calls `onMounted` after two `await`s, and the hook still ran for the right component. Why?

choices.text: The compiler wrapped each `await` to put the current component back after it
choices.why: Right. `_withAsyncContext` saves the component before the `await` and restores it afterwards.

choices.text: `<Suspense>` runs the setup a second time once the data is in
choices.why: Setup ran once per course: the transcript has one `mounted` line for each.

choices.text: A hook registered late is given to whichever component mounts next
choices.why: That would attach it to the wrong component, which is the very failure lesson 10 described.

choices.text: `fetch` keeps track of the component that called it
choices.why: `fetch` is the browser's and knows nothing of Vue; the compiler's wrapper does the work.

prompt: A results list refilters as the student types, and its component loads with a top-level `await` under a `<Suspense>`. Why does the lesson point elsewhere for this?

choices.text: Suspense would show its fallback again on every keystroke, and the list would flicker
choices.why: The opposite: once resolved, it does not go back to the fallback by default.

choices.text: A resolved Suspense shows no fallback for an update; a watcher and a loading flag do
choices.why: Right. Suspense suits data loaded once; data that changes as somebody types is lesson 10's job.

choices.text: A top-level `await` is refused in a component that receives props
choices.why: `SlowCourse` receives `id` and awaits at the top level, and it worked.

choices.text: A `<Suspense>` holds one async component, and a list has many
choices.why: The demo held two, and waited for both.

prompt: `SlowCourse` failed to parse the guitar notes. What caught the error?

choices.text: A `#error` slot on the `<Suspense>`
choices.why: `<Suspense>` has no error slot; the error state is a component's job.

choices.text: `app.config.errorHandler`, which is the first to hear of any error
choices.why: The application's handler comes last, and here it heard nothing, because the hook returned `false`.

choices.text: `ErrorsDemo`'s `onErrorCaptured`
choices.why: Right. It is the nearest ancestor with the hook, and it stored the message.

choices.text: The `await` in `SlowCourse`, which turns a rejection into `undefined`
choices.why: An `await` on a rejection throws; the error left `SlowCourse` and travelled up.

prompt: Returning ___ from the `onErrorCaptured` callback stops the error from going further up, to `app.config.errorHandler`.
An application has one `onErrorCaptured` boundary, at its root, which swaps the whole page for a message. A small widget's request fails. What does the lesson say goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing is caught, because the hook sees only direct children
choices.why: It runs for errors in any descendant, however deep.

choices.text: The widget alone shows the message and the page keeps working
choices.why: That is what a boundary placed around the widget would give.

choices.text: Vue refuses to mount an app with a boundary at the root
choices.why: Vue mounts it; the trouble only shows when something fails.

choices.text: A small failure turns into a blank application
choices.why: Right. Put the boundary where the student can still do something, around the part that failed.

prompt: In the fade demo, what does Vue itself animate?

choices.text: Nothing; the CSS does
choices.why: Right. Vue puts classes on at the right moment and takes them off at `transitionend`.

choices.text: The paragraph's opacity, from 0 to 1, over 600 milliseconds
choices.why: The stylesheet asked for that; Vue only put the classes on and took them off.

choices.text: Only the leave, because CSS animates an entering element on its own
choices.why: It is the leave that CSS cannot do alone: `v-if` would delete the element before it faded.

choices.text: The `display` property, between `none` and `block`
choices.why: That would be `v-show`'s own switch, and it does not animate either.

prompt: Without reduced motion, how many milliseconds did `after-enter` say the fade's enter took?
Mid-fade, the paragraph carried `fade-enter-active fade-enter-to`. Where was `fade-enter-from`?
hint: Look at the *when* column of the table.

choices.text: Waiting to go on at the end, as the state the element fades into
choices.why: That is `fade-enter-to`, the target state. `-from` is the start.

choices.text: On the `<Transition>` element, which wraps the paragraph
choices.why: `<Transition>` draws no element of its own; the classes go on the child.

choices.text: Folded by the browser into `fade-enter-active`
choices.why: The browser folds no classes; Vue removed it.

choices.text: Gone already: it is on for the first frame only
choices.why: Right. It sets the starting state, then comes off at the second frame, when `-to` goes on.

prompt: `v-if` turns false on an element wrapped in `<Transition name="fade">`. When does the element leave the DOM?

choices.text: At once, and the leave classes animate a copy Vue leaves in its place
choices.why: There is no copy: Vue keeps the element itself in the page while it leaves.

choices.text: After one second, the time Vue gives every leave
choices.why: Vue gives no fixed time; it reads the duration from the computed style.

choices.text: When the parent next re-renders for some other reason
choices.why: The removal is tied to the transition, not to the parent's next render.

choices.text: When the transition `fade-leave-active` declares has ended, as read from the computed style
choices.why: Right. That is the one thing CSS alone cannot do: animate an element `v-if` is about to delete.

prompt: After *Add one at the top*, the two old rows carried `slide-move`. Why?

choices.text: Each was pushed one place down by the new row
choices.why: Right. A row that only changes place gets `-move`; the new one got the enter classes.

choices.text: They were taken out and put back, so they were moved
choices.why: They kept their keys and were kept; a row put back would get `-enter-` classes.

choices.text: `-move` goes on every row of the list whenever the list changes
choices.why: The new row had `slide-enter-active slide-enter-to`, not `slide-move`.

choices.text: Their `:key` is the index, which every insert at the top changes
choices.why: Their key is `s.id`, which an insert does not change.

prompt: Which of these are rules the lesson gives for `<TransitionGroup>`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every item needs a real `:key`
choices.why: Right. The move is computed per key.

choices.text: Without `tag`, it always wraps the items in a `<span>`
choices.why: Without `tag`, it draws no wrapper of its own.

choices.text: `tag` names the element drawn around the items
choices.why: Right. Here a `<ul>`, so it is still a list to a screen reader.

choices.text: The items must be `<li>` elements
choices.why: The planner's items are `SessionRow` components; any element or component with a key will do.

choices.text: The `-move` class needs a `transition` in the CSS
choices.why: Right. Without one, the class goes on and nothing is told to animate.

prompt: A `<TransitionGroup>` list keys its rows by index, and an item is inserted at the top. What happens to the old rows?
hint: What does a key follow: the item, or the place?

choices.text: They slide down, exactly as with ids
choices.why: Sliding needs keys that follow the items; an index follows the place.

choices.text: Vue refuses to render the group until the rows have ids
choices.why: Nothing is refused; the list draws, and the animation is what is lost.

choices.text: Each appears to change in place instead of moving
choices.why: Right. Each key now holds a different item, so nothing moved by the keys' account.

choices.text: They move twice, once for the insert and once for the new index
choices.why: A move is computed once per change; here the keys say nothing moved at all.

prompt: With `--reduced-motion`, the fade's enter took about 0 ms. What made it that short?

choices.text: Vue reads `prefers-reduced-motion` and skips every `<Transition>`
choices.why: Vue reads no preference; the stylesheet's media query did the work.

choices.text: The browser dropped the `<Transition>`
choices.why: A browser knows nothing of `<Transition>`, which is Vue's, and the hooks still ran.

choices.text: `transition: none` left no duration in the computed style, so Vue finished at once
choices.why: Right. With no duration to wait for, Vue ran the hooks and the element simply appeared.

choices.text: The `wait 1000` step let the fade run out of sight
choices.why: The hook printed before `wait 1000` began.

prompt:
Why does the planner's week page keep a `

` under the list?

choices.text: To hold the title the dialog's `aria-labelledby` points at
choices.why: The title is the dialog's own `<h2>`, with an id from `useId()`.

choices.text: So that what was added is heard after the focus goes back to the button
choices.why: Right. The focus returns to *Add a session*, and the status line announces the new session.

choices.text: Because `close()` refuses to run while the status line is empty
choices.why: `close()` has no such condition; `onAdded` sets the message and closes the dialog.

choices.text: To announce a failed request, as `role="alert"` did in the errors demo
choices.why: It shows `added`, the message `SessionForm` sends when a session was saved.

prompt: Match each built-in component to what it does in this lesson.

pairs.right: draws its contents at another place in the document
shows a fallback until its async children are ready
puts classes on one element that comes and goes
gives a move class to items that change place

right_distractors: moves the focus into a modal and back

prompt: The planner's `<dialog>` is opened with `showModal()` and also sits inside a `<Teleport to="body">`. By the lesson, what is the Teleport for?
hint: What does the top layer already do?

choices.text: Without it, the panel's `overflow` would clip the dialog
choices.why: A modal dialog is on the top layer, above any `overflow` or `z-index`, teleported or not.

choices.text: Keeping the dialog out of the markup of the component that opens it
choices.why: Right. Drawing it on top is the top layer's work; the Teleport only tidies where it sits in the page.

choices.text: Moving the focus into the dialog
choices.why: Teleport never moves the focus; `showModal()` does.

choices.text: Making the page behind the dialog inert, so it cannot be clicked
choices.why: That is `showModal()` as well: the inert page comes with the top layer.

prompt: `PlannerDialog` exposes `open`, and calling it runs `dialog.value.___()` on the native element.
hint: The method that puts it on the top layer.
